claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayers undergo progressive plastic deformation under sustained elevated-temperature loading.
The progressive deformation is governed by differential creep of soft FCC layers and hard BCC layers.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order in the FCC layers elevate the activation energy for dislocation motion, especially dislocation climb.
The elevated barriers to dislocation motion produce greater accumulated plastic strain and localized interfacial slip or shear banding.
The starting coating contains alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
The starting alloy has significant lattice distortion and measurable short-range order.
A sustained constant load should be applied at 600–900 °C while preserving the nanoscale layered structure.
Dislocation climb is active in the proposed 600–900 °C testing regime.
Interface coherency, interfacial bonding quality, and short-range-order-induced local structure govern the creep response.
The FCC layers primarily accommodate deformation through thermally activated dislocation climb and glide.
Lattice distortion and short-range order cause dislocation accumulation and stress concentration at FCC/BCC interfaces.
The hard BCC layers obstruct dislocations, causing interfacial pile-ups and localized shear.
Interfacial pile-ups and localized shear progressively deform the entire multilayer.
Initially homogeneous creep deformation will evolve into localized interfacial slip.
Dislocation density will increase preferentially in the FCC layers during creep.
Creep will produce FCC/BCC interfacial dislocation pile-ups and may produce interface decohesion or shear bands.
Loaded samples will have more plastic strain than the undeformed starting baseline.
The as-fabricated multilayer has low initial dislocation density and uniformly bonded interfaces.
The proposed mechanism is limited to temperatures high enough for climb but low enough to avoid significant interdiffusion or recrystallization.
The response may change substantially with layer thickness, interface quality, or temperature.
